title: Tomy Tutor Play Computer
subtitle: a kids' programming toy that scaffolds the edit-compile-run loop into three discrete physical keys — 'Programme', 'Step', and 'Run' — so a child builds a four-line program, steps through it line by line, then watches it animate
why_scout_cares: The Tomy Tutor Play Computer (1984) is a distinctive early kids' programming toy because it makes the programming cycle tactile and explicit. Instead of a display-heavy computer, it uses a printed 'program sheet' the child positions in a window, a four-button control to enter commands, and a small set of physical keys including PROGRAMME, STEP and RUN. The child assembles a short program (of roughly four steps), then presses STEP to execute it one line at a time, then RUN to play the whole sequence as an animation on the small VFD/LED area. This is a genuine scaffolded version of the edit-run-debug loop, executed in hardware keys rather than on-screen, and it predates the visual-programming-for-kids wave. It is held in the collection of the Victoria and Albert Museum (object number MISC.360:1,2-1987).

research.title: Tomy Tutor Play Computer
research.overview: The Tomy Tutor Play Computer (1984) is a handheld kids' programming toy that turns the edit-compile-run loop into a physical sequence of button presses. Rather than a screen-centric computer, the toy works with a printed program sheet that slides into a window, a control cluster of navigation keys, and dedicated PROGRAMME, STEP, and RUN keys. The child constructs a short program of around four steps by choosing from a limited command set, presses STEP to execute the program one line at a time (reviewing each step), then presses RUN to play the whole program as a moving animation. A surviving example is held in the Victoria and Albert Museum's collection (object number MISC.360:1,2-1987).

deepDive.heading: The physical programming loop
deepDive.text: The toy makes the stages of programming legible as hardware. The child enters commands with a four-button control, builds a program of about four lines on a printed program sheet, then uses a STEP key to run the program one instruction at a time — reviewing each step — before a RUN key executes the whole thing as an animation. This scaffolds the edit-run-debug cycle into discrete, labelled physical actions rather than abstract on-screen commands.

deepDive.heading: Why it matters
deepDive.text: Most children's computing toys of the era (Speak & Spell, the micro:bit's predecessors) taught drill or vocabulary; the Tutor Play Computer is unusual in explicitly teaching the programming cycle as an embodied, stepped ritual. It is a tangible-programming ancestor of later physical programming toys and belongs beside the museum's other kids' computing entries.
